issues.legal_issue: A tenant who has attorned to an assignee of the original landlord cannot challenge the assignee’s derivative title in an eviction suit, and the landlord need not prove title as in a title suit.
material_facts: The premises had originally been let by the former owner, whose undertaking and premises later vested successively in a public authority and an assignee by operation of law.
The tenant paid rent to the public authority for many years after the first transfer.
After the premises transferred to the assignee, the tenant was informed of the transfer, offered to pay rent to the assignee, and sought in a separate suit to have the assignee accept rent.
The tenant did not respond to the assignee’s notice terminating the tenancy, and its pleadings in the separate suit acknowledged the assignee’s ownership.
The summary eviction suit was supported by transfer documents and the tenant’s conduct and admissions.
issues.conclusion: The assignee’s ownership and the tenant’s attornment were sufficiently established for the eviction suit; there was no genuine title dispute requiring an elaborate trial, and the tenant could not rely on its challenge to the assignee’s derivative title.
issues.legal_principle: In an eviction suit, a landlord is not required to establish ownership as fully as in a title suit (Sheela v. Firm Prahlad Rai Prem Prakash; Boorugu Mahadev & Sons v. Sirigiri Narasing Rao). Under Section 116 of the Evidence Act, a tenant is estopped from denying the landlord’s title, although a tenant may challenge an assignee’s derivative title if the tenant has not attorned to the assignee. Paying rent to or otherwise accepting the assignee’s title establishes attornment and bars that challenge (Bismillah De v. Majeed Shah). Attornment continues the existing tenancy rather than creating a new one (Uppalapati Veera Venkata Satyanarayanaraju v. Josyula Hanumayamma).

rule.if: summary_eviction_suit and ownership_transferred_to_assignee and tenant_paid_rent_to_predecessor and tenant_accepted_assignee

predicates.summary_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a summary suit to evict a tenant from leased premises.
predicates.ownership_transferred_to_assignee: The premises passed from the original landlord to an assignee through a documented transfer.
predicates.tenant_paid_rent_to_predecessor: The tenant paid rent to a successor landlord before the assignee acquired the premises.
predicates.tenant_accepted_assignee: The tenant offered to pay rent to, or otherwise acknowledged, the assignee as landlord.
predicates.assignee_title_and_attornment_establishe: The assignee’s title and the tenant’s attornment are sufficiently established to defeat the tenant’s challenge to derivative title.

issues.definition: When a summary eviction suit follows a documented transfer and the tenant paid rent to a predecessor and accepted the assignee, the assignee’s title and attornment are established.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who receives a notice terminating the tenancy and fails to object to its validity at the first available opportunity waives that objection.
material_facts: The tenant received the landlord’s notice terminating the tenancy and demanding rent and possession.
The tenant did not reply to the notice or raise an objection to its validity at that time.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s failure to object at the first available opportunity amounted to waiver of an objection to the notice’s validity or infirmity.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, an objection to the validity or infirmity of a tenancy-termination notice must be raised specifically and at the earliest opportunity; otherwise it is deemed waived. The Court relied on Parwati Bai v. Radhika.

predicates.tenancy_termination_notice_received: A tenant received a notice from the landlord terminating the tenancy.
predicates.no_timely_notice_objection: The tenant did not specifically object to the notice’s validity at the first available opportunity.
predicates.notice_objection_waived: The tenant is treated as having waived an objection to the notice’s validity or infirmity.

issues.definition: When a tenant receives a termination notice and does not object to it at the first available opportunity, the objection is waived.

issues.legal_issue: The documentary evidence established that the recurring payment for the premises was rent rather than a smaller rent separated from maintenance charges.
material_facts: The tenant had paid the same total monthly amount to the prior landlord over a long period.
The rent receipts produced by the parties showed the total amount as monthly rent.
The tenant claimed that only a smaller portion was rent and the balance was maintenance charges, but the Court found that division unsupported by the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The monthly rent was the total amount shown by the payment history and rent receipts, not the smaller amount asserted by the tenant.
issues.legal_principle: The Court determined the rent from the parties’ payment history and documentary evidence, including the rent receipts, and rejected an unsupported division of the recurring payment into rent and maintenance charges.

predicates.summary_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a summary suit to evict a tenant from leased premises.
predicates.tenant_paid_combined_amount_as_rent: The tenant had regularly paid the combined recurring amount to the prior landlord as rent.
predicates.rent_receipts_support_combined_amount: The rent receipts produced by the parties recorded the combined recurring amount as rent.
predicates.combined_amount_was_monthly_rent: The combined recurring amount was the monthly rent for the premises.

issues.definition: When a tenant regularly paid a combined amount as rent and the rent receipts support that treatment, the combined amount is the monthly rent.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may pursue eviction under the general property-tenancy law when non-residential premises fall outside the applicable premises-tenancy statute because their monthly rent exceeds its prescribed limit.
material_facts: The premises were let for a non-residential purpose in an area covered by the premises-tenancy statute.
The Court found that the monthly rent exceeded the statute’s prescribed limit.
The landlord brought the summary eviction suit under the Transfer of Property Act and the applicable original-side rules.
issues.conclusion: The premises-tenancy statute did not apply, and the landlord was entitled to bring the summary suit under the Transfer of Property Act and the applicable rules.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(f) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997 excludes non-residential premises in the relevant municipal areas when their monthly rent exceeds the prescribed limit. The Court therefore held that the suit was maintainable under the Transfer of Property Act read with Rule 1(B) of the Calcutta High Court Rules; the request for leave to defend was assessed under Rules 6 and 9.

predicates.summary_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a summary suit to evict a tenant from leased premises.
predicates.premises_used_for_nonresidential_purpose: The tenant used the premises for a non-residential purpose.
predicates.monthly_rent_exceeds_statutory_limit: The monthly rent exceeded the limit that determines whether the premises-tenancy statute applies.
predicates.premises_tenancy_statute_inapplicable: The premises-tenancy statute does not govern the premises, leaving the general property-tenancy law available for the eviction suit.

issues.definition: If a summary eviction suit concerns non-residential premises whose monthly rent exceeds the applicable limit, the premises-tenancy statute does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Leave to defend a summary eviction suit is not warranted when the tenant’s proposed defenses are neither arguable nor supported by a substantial factual or legal basis.
material_facts: The tenant sought leave to defend on grounds concerning the landlord’s title and attornment, the amount of rent, and the choice of tenancy law.
The transfer documents, rent receipts, payment history, correspondence, and the tenant’s own pleadings addressed those grounds.
The Court found that the proposed defenses lacked an arguable or substantial basis and did not require an elaborate trial.
The appellate court had granted unconditional leave and remanded the suit, while the first-instance judge had denied leave and entered an eviction decree.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to leave to defend; the appeal was allowed, the appellate judgment was set aside, and the first-instance order and eviction decree were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rules 6 and 9 of the Calcutta High Court Rules, leave to defend a summary suit is not justified where the defendant raises no arguable and substantial defense requiring trial. The Court concluded that the tenant’s three grounds had no factual or legal foundation for trial.

predicates.summary_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a summary suit to evict a tenant from leased premises.
predicates.defenses_contradicted_by_record: The tenant’s proposed defenses were contradicted or answered by documents, payment history, correspondence, or the tenant’s own conduct and admissions.
predicates.no_arguable_substantial_defense: The tenant raised no defense with an arguable and substantial factual or legal basis requiring a trial.
predicates.leave_to_defend_denied: The tenant is denied leave to defend the summary suit.

issues.definition: When a tenant in a summary eviction suit relies on defenses contradicted by the record and raises no arguable substantial defense, leave to defend is denied.
